newsitem.title: GREECE: Greek farmers take their protest to Athens.
newsitem.headline: Greek farmers take their protest to Athens.

text.p: Greek farmers take their 22-day-old protest to Athens on Thursday with a midday rally outside the parliament building to press for a meeting with Prime Minister Costas Simitis.

"About 150 buses will travel to Athens. We will march to parliament and ask for a meeting with the prime minister. This is his chance to show that he cares about our problems," farmers' representative Vangelis Boutas told reporters.
Simitis has flatly rejected the farmers' demands for cheaper fuel, equipment and state subsidies on products, saying next year's budget can't afford the cost estimated at $4 billion.

He has ruled out a meeting with the farmers before they abandon their three-week blockade of the main north-south highway and warned other striking state workers that there is no spare money for higher salaries or bonuses.
"If Mr Simitis doesn't meet us to discuss our demands we will go back to the barricades," Boutas said. "The government holds the key to end the blockade."
The number of barricades set up by the farmers have dwindled in recent days with only three main ones still going strong in central and and northern Greece.

Agriculture minister Stephanos Tzoumakas said on Wednesday the European Union had agreed to allow Greece to divert $40 million in agricultural development funds towards paying for crops damaged by weather.

That was not among the main demands of the farmers but would be welcome news for many hard hit by recent storms. Cotton farmers in the central Thessaly region and northern Thrace have lost crops and complained compensation was too small.
Simitis's tough 1997 budget has angered workers by clamping down on state hiring, limiting wage rises for another year, levying new taxes and eliminating hundreds of tax breaks.
Simitis has said the strict budget is essential to meet economic targets so Greece can join a single European currency by the year 2001.

"If by the year 2,001 we don't catch Europe's train we risk losing everything we gained through our (Eurpean Union) membership in the past 15 years," National Economy and Finance Minister Yannos Papandoniou told parliament on Wednesday during a debate on the budget.
The government hopes to gain about $4 million next year from the abolition of the tax breaks and the introduction of new taxes, but the unpopular measures prompted strikes by many working groups.
Continuing strikes by seamen have left ships docked at ports around Greece for the third day. State doctors, tax, customs and finance ministry employees also went on strike on Wednesday.
Civil aviation unions, except air traffic controllers, have annnounced a 24-hour strike on Friday that is sure to disrupt flight schedules.

The strike wave was expected to ease after parliament votes on the budget on Saturday. Simitis' PASOK Socialist party has an absolute majority of 163 deputies in the 300-seat house and was expected to pass the budget without problems.
